AFDRAH

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Raleigh NC
252 AM EDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

* Reduced POP for Sunday, raised MaxT Sunday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 252 PM Friday...

1) Very warm and humid today, with scattered, mainly PM 
showers/thunderstorms. Last shot at significant rain through the 
week. 

2) Sunday is trending drier, a bit hotter. Dry with temperatures 
closer to seasonable values much of next week. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 252 AM Saturday...

1) Very warm and humid today, with scattered, mainly PM 
showers/thunderstorms. Last chance of significant rain for a while!

The upper level short wave trough will move from the Tennessee 
Valley east across the Appalachians and over our region through 
tonight. The base of the trough will move east of the area Sunday 
morning. 

At the surface, a weak cold front (likely consisting of old 
convective boundaries) was located from west to east, generally 
along the US-64 corridor from just south of the Triad to the 
southern part of the Triangle areas. PW's were analyzed at 1.75 in 
the western Piedmont to 2+ inches in the NE Coastal Plain. Dew 
points and surface temperatures were generally in the lower to mid 
70s. Earlier lingering showers have all dissipated, with plenty of 
mid and high clouds around. There were areas of low stratus 
developing.

Some earlier 00z/CAMS were forecasting some showers/storms this 
morning. It appears they were tied to old MCV's and disturbances 
left over from Friday's storms upstream. However, with the activity 
now all but gone, the latest CAMS suggest that it will be mostly low 
stratus and some fog through 13z or so that will prevail. There is 
little indicating of any additional showers through mid-morning. 

However, as the stratus breaks we are expecting fairly aggressive 
heating today into the lower to mid 80s by noon. As the short wave 
aloft approaches, expect areas of showers and thunderstorms to 
develop, especially after noon. The higher POP should be between 200 
PM and 900 PM. QPF continues to show a lot of variability, but 
averages around 0.5 in Piedmont. Locally heavy rain is expected to 
affect some areas, but just as many will not see any rainfall. 

There should still be scattered storms this evening, even possibly 
linger into the night in the east. 

2) Sunday trending drier, a bit hotter. Mainly dry with temps closer 
to seasonable values much of next week.  

With the base of the short wave trough expected to pass east toward 
the coast before heating Sunday and the surface front to not be far 
behind, it appears Sunday will bring drier weather and hotter 
temperatures than today. Readings should reach the upper 80s to 
around 90. In addition, the showers are expected to be along the 
coast for the most part. 

Most of next week will be dry and cooler thanks to an upper ridge 
that will be positioned to our west much of the time, with surface 
high pressure to our north and northeast. This will result in a low 
level NE flow and highs in the 80s. Lows should dip into the 60s 
for the most part.  

&&

.AVIATION /06Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/... 
As of 142 AM Saturday...

VFR will largely prevail across central NC trough 06z-09z, with low 
stratus expected to develop over central NC. All terminals likely to 
experience IFR conditions. A period of LIFR is even possible around 
daybreak, along with patchy MVFR/IFR visibilities. VFR will return 
to most areas by midday on Saturday, but MVFR may linger into early 
afternoon around the Triad. Showers and storms are then expected to 
develop in the afternoon across the region, and they should be more 
widespread compared to today. Brief gusty winds and sub-VFR 
conditions will be possible with any storms.

Outlook: Shower and thunderstorm chances will continue through this 
evening as a cold front makes its way through central NC.
Low stratus and/or fog may develop and cause sub-VFR restrictions 
again on Sunday and Monday mornings as well. 

&&

.RAH WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

DISCUSSION...Badgett
AVIATION...Badgett/Danco

AFDILM

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Wilmington NC
234 AM EDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Updated today's forecast based on the latest guidance for timing
of showers and storms. Models continue to be consistent on the
strength and timing of a cold front on Monday. The only change
to the forecast during this update was to increase wind speeds 
behind the cold front on Monday evening. Wind gusts have also
been increased over the marine forecast zones with warm SSTs. 
Dry high pressure will follow, so forecast changes were minimal
through next week.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge aloft will 
maintain good chances for showers and thunderstorms through 
Sunday.

2) Well-above normal temperatures and high humidity will 
maintain daytime heat indices at or above 100 degrees through 
Monday.

3) A modified Canadian airmass should bring near-normal 
temperatures beginning Tuesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1... Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge 
aloft will maintain good chances for showers and thunderstorms 
through Sunday.

Deep Gulf moisture in place over the Carolinas and above-normal
temperatures will produce widespread showers and thunderstorms
this afternoon. High resolution models have maintained poor 
consistency each hour. Surface convergence along the sea breeze 
is likely to be the main initiator of convection after noon. A 
few isolated showers are possible in coastal southeast NC this 
morning due to onshore flow. Weak shortwave energy lifting 
northward through the Carolinas suggests that some development 
is possible during the afternoon for inland areas in additional 
to surface convergence along the sea breeze. This lift is weak 
and would favor the NC/SC border and points northward into the 
Sandhills. 

Weak shear should keep the potential for severe weather low.
Some heavy rain is possible given the near record PW and
slow storm motions.

Drier air moves into the mountains and western Piedmont on
Sunday, but the moisture-laden atmosphere will largely remain in
tact near the coast. The upper trough producing the break in 
the ridge should slide eastward across the Carolinas, perhaps 
enhancing bulk shear to around 20 knots. Multicells should 
become possible, perhaps bringing better potential for gusty 
winds. The upper trough should shift offshore Sunday night ahead
of rising mid and upper level heights spreading eastward from 
the Mid South.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Well-above normal temperatures and high 
humidity will maintain daytime heat indices at or above 100 
degrees through Monday.

Above-normal temperatures continue to sit near the 90th
percentile for mid September. Deep moisture should produce
widespread cloudiness in addition to convection this weekend.
These factors will keep heat indices below the 105 degree
threshold for heat advisories. 

Ensemble spread for 850 temperatures remains low through Monday,
the latest forecast keeps forecast highs in the upper 80s to 
around 90 through Monday. With dewpoints well into the 70s, heat
indices will remain in the 100-103 range through Monday. Monday
is expected to be the warmest of these days with decreased
cloudiness.

NWS ILM has never issued a Heat Advisory later than September 5
since the introduction of VTEC product codes twenty years ago. 
(and that latest advisory was earlier this month)


KEY MESSAGE 3...A modified Canadian airmass should bring near-normal 
temperatures beginning Tuesday.

Models have all come into line over the past 24 hours showing 
the strongest Canadian high we've seen since last Spring moving 
across New England Tuesday into Wednesday. This should push a 
cold front southward across the eastern Carolinas Monday night, 
allowing a modified Canadian airmass to spread across the area 
Tuesday into Wednesday. This won't be crisp, dry Canadian air by
any means given its long passage across water temps in the 70s 
and 80s, but it should bring cooler air across the area knocking
temperatures back down closer to normal for mid September.

Forecast lows in particular look refreshing with 60s expected
for all but east-facing beaches Tuesday night and Wednesday
night. Some inland locations could conceivably dip to 60
degrees.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Rest of Tonight... Mixing should maintain VFR for coastal 
terminals, but can't rule out some brief MVFR CIGs. Light 
boundary layer winds, wet soils, and enhanced low level moisture
should produce IFR across a large portion of inland terminals. 
Expect some CIGs to reach LIFR by sunrise. Light wind should 
mix-out restrictions a couple of hours after sunrise.

Saturday... Isolated showers near the NC coast may product 
brief restrictions at ILM this morning (around sunrise). As the 
sea breeze deepens during the early afternoon, convection should
mature near the coast and gradually push inland through the 
afternoon. Additional development is possible inland during the 
early afternoon. Most areas are expected to see impacts from 
thunderstorms by the end of the day as showers become 
widespread.

Extended Outlook... Scattered showers and thunderstorms 
bringing brief MVFR/IFR conditions are expected to continue 
into Saturday evening. Some showers are possible on Sunday, but 
coverage should be less than previous days. There is also a low 
potential for late night/early morning stratus or ground fog 
affecting KLBT and KFLO late Saturday night and again late 
Sunday night. VFR conditions should prevail Monday through 
Wednesday as a more stable and drier Canadian airmass builds in 
from the northeast.

&&

.MARINE...
Southerly flow will continue to supply a warm and humid air 
mass through the weekend. This moisture-laden air mass will 
bring multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms both Saturday
and Sunday night. Southerly winds around 10-15 knots. The sea 
breeze will produce localized enhancement of gusts to 20 knots 
each afternoon.

Drier weather should develop on Monday evening as high pressure
strengthens aloft over the Carolinas. The strongest Canadian
high we've seen since last Spring should move across New England
Tuesday and Wednesday, pushing a cold front southward across the
Carolina coastal waters Monday night. Northeast winds behind the
front should increase to a solid 20 knots offshore and 15-20 
knots nearshore Tuesday into Tuesday night. Seas within 20 
miles of shore could build to 4-6 feet with dominant wave
periods near 6 seconds.

&&

.ILM WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
NC...Coastal Flood Advisory from 10 AM this morning to 1 PM EDT 
     this afternoon for NCZ107.
SC...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Jacksonville FL
235 AM EDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

For the latest NE FL and SE GA Daily Key Messages please visit:
https:/www.weather.gov/media/jax/briefings/nws-jax-briefing.pdf

- Numerous Afternoon and Evening Thunderstorms Expected Today.
  Isolated Strong Storm Potential Along the I-95 Corridor During
  the Afternoon Hours. Stronger Storms May Produce Wind Gusts of
  40-50 mph, Frequent Lightning Strikes, and Torrential 
  Downpours that Could Result in Localized Flooding.

- Daily Peak Heat Index Values of 107 Degrees Expected through 
  Monday.

- Scattered Afternoon and Evening Thunderstorms Are Expected
  from Sunday through Wednesday.

- Moderate Rip Current Risk Continues at All Area Beaches
  through Monday. High Risk more likely from Tuesday through 
  Thursday as Breezy Onshore Winds Develop at Coastal Locations.
  

&&

.NEAR TERM /TODAY THROUGH TONIGHT/...
Main Highlights:

- Potential for isolated strong thunderstorms and localized flooding 
today

Persistent, deep southwest flow continues today with PWATs remaining 
elevated at about 2.2 to 2.4 inches across the entire area. The 18z 
sounding from JAX measured 2.31 inches of PWAT and has not changed 
much from that value since Thursday. The 500 mb temps remain on the 
warm side about -5.5C, and does not change appreciably today. 
Surface winds will be fairly light from the southwest and west so 
west and east coast sea breezes will be moving inland during the 
day. This should result in initial development of showers and storms 
west of I-75 during late morning hours. Merging of the southwest 
flow/west coast sea breeze and the east coast sea breeze should 
result in isolated strong storms for the eastern zones. Main 
concerns will be strong gusty winds and heavy rainfall. DCAPE 
remains on the low side at about 600 J/kg today. Effective rain 
producing storms will be capable of localized flooding especially in 
poor drainage and urbanized locations. Scattered convection will be 
ongoing in the evening with most of the activity forecast to be 
across southeast GA, but should be quite weak at 8-9 PM after the 
airmass has been worked over. Only a few sprinkles anticipated
by midnight per latest hi-resolution models. 

High temperatures today will be in the lower 90s, with max afternoon 
heat index values peaking around 102-107. 

Patchy fog, locally dense fog at times, is expected early this 
morning and again late tonight for the inland areas.

&&

.SHORT TERM /SUNDAY THROUGH MONDAY NIGHT/...
Main Highlights This Period:

- Daily Thunderstorm Potential Sunday and Monday

Prevailing flow will shift about to become more out of the northeast 
by Monday night as ridging moves northward and high pressure 
rotation forms north of Georgia. Diurnal convection will become 
inhibited over southeast Georgia as drier air and high pressure 
ridging extends into the northern portion of the forecast area, 
inhibiting the development of showers and storms, with storms more 
likely to form over north central Florida and for areas south of the 
I-10 corridor. High temperatures will rise up into the lower 90s 
this weekend with overnight low temperatures dropping down into the 
lower to mid 70s over inland areas and int the mid to upper 70s for 
areas along the coast. Heat index values today will rise to over 
100 with apparent temperatures potentially reaching as high as 110 
for parts of northeast Florida, however conditions are anticipated 
to remain below heat advisory criteria. Potential for patchy early 
morning fog and low cloud decks over inland areas before and around 
sunrise during the overnight and early morning hours this weekend.

&&

.LONG TERM /TUESDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Main Highlights This Period: 

- Daily Thunderstorms Potential Each Day Next Week

- Elevated Rip Current Risk Next Week 

Northeasterly onshore flow will be in place through the majority of 
next week as the axis of high pressure rotation to the north 
gradually moves towards the west. Breezy onshore winds will bring 
showers and isolated thunderstorms in the mornings, with coverage 
expanding inland throughout each day. Above average high 
temperatures reaching into the lower 90s will gradually drop down 
into the upper 80s and be nearer the seasonal average by midweek. 
Heat index values will drop down to be below 100.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z SATURDAY THROUGH 06Z SUNDAY/...
LIFR conditions developed at JAX and VQQ with a chance of IFR for 
GNV. The CIGS and VIS may bounce around through 12Z. Overall, much 
lower chances of any CIGS and IFR for the coastal sites towards 
sunrise. VFR should be present by 13z-14z, scattered cumulus 
developing into the mid to late morning hours. Another round of 
showers and storms expected again today, likely starting by about 
16z, and then become more numerous during the afternoon and early 
evening. Have TEMPO and PROB30 groups TSRA for the time periods from 
about 18z-24z at all terminals. Timing may need to be refined in 
subsequent forecasts. Sfc winds light southwest to west, with east 
coast sea breeze developing at SGJ, CRG, and SSI by the mid to 
late afternoon hours.

&&

.MARINE...

Weakening high pressure south of the area will maintain south to 
southwest winds and afternoon sea breezes through the weekend. Daily 
mid to late afternoon thunderstorms will move offshore, bringing 
locally strong wind gusts and frequent lightning at times. On 
Tuesday, high pressure ridge will push south along the east coast 
and push a cold front south through the area waters, creating 
strengthening northeast winds and building seas. This may lead to a 
small craft advisory for portions of the coastal waters starting 
Tuesday and may continue into Wednesday and Thursday.

Rip Currents: Prevailing offshore winds (except for an afternoon 
sea breeze) and weak easterly swells will keep a low-end moderate 
risk of rip currents in effect the next couple of days. 
Strengthening northeast winds late Monday night into Tuesday will 
likely result in a high risk at all area beaches through at least 
Thursday as breakers build.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...

Diurnal southwesterly winds will persist through the weekend and 
then shifting to become out of the northeast next week. As a result 
of the moist southwesterly flow, the diurnal east coast sea breeze 
will be pinned near the shoreline and not reach inland much past the 
I-95 corridor. Flow pattern is expected to shift to become more 
onshore by Tuesday of next week.

Light surface and transport winds on Sunday will result in poor to 
fair daytime dispersion.

Fog Potential: Gusty and erratic wind shifts will occur from 
thunderstorm activity. Patchy fog is expected across inland areas 
the next couple of mornings, with widespread dense fog unlikely.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...

As far as rainfall today into tonight, areal amounts of around 0.2 
to 0.5 inches are forecast. Many areas may see less than that. 
However, model guidance shows some amounts of about 3 inches are
possible in a few pockets mainly over the eastern zones, but 
also shown to be possible toward Alachua and Marion counties. As
such, where these heavy rains occur today, temporary flooding 
is possible, especially in any poor drainage or urbanized areas.

&&

.PRELIMINARY POINT TEMPS/POPS...
AMG  91  73  92  72 /  50  30  20   0 
SSI  89  77  91  77 /  60  30  30  10 
JAX  91  74  92  75 /  70  20  50  10 
SGJ  90  75  91  75 /  60  20  50  20 
GNV  91  73  91  74 /  70  20  50  10 
OCF  92  74  92  74 /  60  20  60  20 

&&

.JAX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
FL...None.
GA...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

FXUS65 KBOU 120823
AFDBOU

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
223 AM MDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Slightly cooler today, then unseasonably warm along the Front
  Range and I-25 Corridor Sunday. Isolated showers and storms, but
  some uptick over the mountains Sunday. 

- Unsettled pattern next week, with cooler weather arriving by
  Tuesday. 

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Friday/...
Issued at 223 AM MDT Sat Sep 12 2026

Cold front has pushed across northeast Colorado in these wee
morning hours. This will support cooler weather today, although 
high temperatures will still be near normal for this time of year.
A couple showers may linger over the northern plains early this 
morning, with redevelopment mainly over the mountains and Palmer 
Divide area this afternoon where airmass is less strongly capped. 
A few of these high based showers and storms could drift onto the 
adjacent plains as usual late in the afternoon/evening, but no 
significant precipitation is expected. 

We'll see low level moisture gradually return to the eastern
plains tonight, with areas of stratus likely developing 
along/east of a Limon to Sterling line. That does offer up some 
uncertainty for Sunday's high temperatures. Lee troughing indeed 
looks slow to develop, and thus the cooler and more moist boundary
layer conditions will likely persist more than most models 
advertise. While Denver and the I-25 Corridor is still shaping up
to be quite hot (lower 90s), somewhat cooler weather will likely 
hold over the eastern plains. While we've trimmed those 
temperatures from previous forecasts, further trimming is quite 
likely for the eastern plains due to the morning stratus and 
deeper moist boundary layer. Regarding convection, the mountains 
will see an uptick in convective coverage and intensity as another
monsoonal moisture plume pushes northeast into the state. 
Precipitable Water values increase to >150% of normal over the 
mountains, and thus a couple stronger storms could produce brief 
heavy rain. They will likely tend to weaken as they attempt to 
move off the higher terrain given locally drier airmass. At this 
time, the prospects of these tapping into the richer air over the
eastern plains also seems slim. 

For Monday, it still looks quite warm with more pronounced lee
troughing and downslope in west-southwest flow aloft. Regarding
convective potential, the plume of mid/upper level moisture shifts
across Colorado, but may end up being pushed too far south/east  
for higher shower/storm coverage. PoPs originating from model 
blends were still rather aggressive but wouldn't be surprised to 
see the higher coverage shift well southeast of the I-76 Corridor,
especially considering the eastward scouring of low level 
moisture ahead of the lee trough. 

Tuesday through Thursday is shaping up to have the highest
coverage of showers/storms for the week ahead. On Tuesday, the
monsoonal moisture plume is advertised to shift northward slightly
as an upper level trough digs into the western U.S. At the same
time, a more significant cold front will be pushing southward
across the plains, lending itself to a stronger low level upslope
component east of the Front Range. High temperatures are still
looking to cool into the 70s, with a 30-40% chance of highs 
holding below 70F on the plains. For Wednesday and Thursday, the 
forecast area would get into a more favorable location for weak 
synoptic scale lift as models are in better agreement with a weak 
shortwave lifting slowly east across the northern Great Basin into
Wyoming. We'll still need a weak front or two to help our upslope
in order to see higher shower/storm coverage, but trends have 
been in our favor here for light to locally moderate precipitation
amounts. Trends would then be for drier weather and near normal 
temperatures for later next week. 

&&

.AVIATION /06Z TAFS through 06Z Sunday/...
Issued at 1149 PM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

Weak prefrontal wind shift will bring VRB winds in the very short
term, then a cold front is scheduled to arrive by 08Z at KDEN 
with a push of gusty north-northeast winds to around 20 kts. 
Front will make it to KAPA by ~09Z, then winds should gradually 
weaken and turn more northeast (more VRB at KBJC and KAPA), before
taking on a more easterly component by 15Z-18Z.

Another round of virga showers will be possible Saturday 
afternoon, likely starting 21Z-22Z. Although conditions look 
slightly less favorable than Friday, a few microbursts with gusty 
winds up to 30KT cannot be ruled out, particularly near KAPA. 
Otherwise, winds will gradually turn more SE-S but could be gusty 
to ~20 kts due to outflows from showers on the Palmer Divide. 
Winds eventually return to fairly normal S-SW by 05Z-06Z Sunday. 

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$
